title: Design a distributed rate limiter
brief: We run a public API behind a fleet of stateless gateway nodes. Design a rate limiting service that enforces per-API-key and per-IP limits consistently across all gateways. Clients that exceed their quota should get a clear 429 response, and the limiter must not become a bottleneck or a single point of failure.
constraints: ~2M distinct API keys, limits configurable per plan tier
Limits like 100 req/s burst and 10k req/hour
Slight over-admission (a few %) is acceptable; hard under-admission is not

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define what is limited (key, IP, endpoint), window semantics, accuracy expectations and behaviour on limiter failure.
keyPoints: Limit dimensions: API key, IP, and optionally endpoint; multiple rules evaluated per request
Support burst plus sustained limits (e.g. per-second and per-hour)
Return 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers
Approximate accuracy acceptable; explicitly state tolerated over-admission
Decide fail-open vs fail-closed when the limiter store is unavailable
Non-goals: billing-grade metering, DDoS scrubbing at L3/L4

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Specify the internal check call the gateway makes and the admin API for configuring limits.
keyPoints: checkAndConsume(key, ruleId, cost=1) -> {allowed, remaining, resetAt}
Batch variant to evaluate several rules in one round trip
Admin CRUD: PUT /limits/{tier} with rate, burst, window
Gateway caches rule config locally with TTL; config pushed on change
Response headers to client: 429, Retry-After, rate limit remaining/reset

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Describe how counters or buckets are stored and how rules are stored.
keyPoints: Token bucket per (key, rule): tokens and lastRefillTs stored in a Redis hash
Alternative sliding window counter: current and previous window counts, weighted interpolation
Keys expire via TTL so idle buckets are reclaimed automatically
Rule config in a durable store (e.g. MongoDB) and cached in memory
Sliding window log (sorted set) is exact but memory-heavy; avoid at this scale

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show the request path from gateway through the limiter and how state is updated atomically.
keyPoints: Gateway middleware calls a Redis cluster directly or via a thin limiter sidecar
Atomic refill-and-decrement in a Lua script so check and update are one operation
Use server time inside Redis (TIME) to avoid gateway clock skew
Local in-process pre-limiter rejects obviously abusive keys without a network hop
Config service publishes rule changes to gateways via pub/sub

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Explain how the counter store scales and how hot keys are handled.
keyPoints: Redis Cluster shards by hash slot of the bucket key; scale by adding shards
Hot key mitigation: split a heavy key into N sub-buckets each with limit/N
Local token leasing: gateway grabs a batch of tokens and spends them locally
Pipeline/batch multiple rule checks to keep one RTT per request
Co-locate limiter shards per region; global limits approximated by per-region quotas

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Cover what happens when Redis nodes fail, are slow, or lose data.
keyPoints: Tight client timeout (~2ms); on timeout fail open for most tiers, fail closed for sensitive endpoints
Redis replica failover may lose recent counts; acceptable brief over-admission
Circuit breaker to stop hammering a degraded shard
Fallback to local per-node limits (global limit / node count) during outages
Monitor rejection rate and limiter latency; alert on sudden shifts

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare algorithms and centralized vs local enforcement.
keyPoints: Token bucket: allows bursts, O(1) state; fixed window: simple but boundary bursts of 2x
Sliding log: exact but O(requests) memory
Centralized store: accurate but adds RTT; local only: fast but inaccurate with many nodes
Token leasing trades accuracy for latency and store load
Durable DB instead of Redis is too slow for per-request writes

modelSummary: Gateways call a sharded Redis Cluster that holds a token bucket per (API key, rule), updated atomically by a Lua script that refills based on Redis server time and decrements in one step. Keys carry TTLs so idle buckets disappear. Rules live in a durable store and are cached in gateways and refreshed via pub/sub. Multiple rules are evaluated in a single pipelined round trip to keep added latency to about 1ms. Hot keys are split into sub-buckets or served by local token leases to avoid overloading one shard. Each check has a tight timeout with a circuit breaker; on failure most traffic fails open with a degraded per-node local limit, while sensitive endpoints fail closed. Failover can lose a few counts, which is acceptable given the stated tolerance. The design trades exactness for low latency and horizontal scalability, and responses include standard 429 and Retry-After headers.

title: Design a URL shortener on a sharded MongoDB cluster
brief: Design a URL shortening service like bit.ly, storing data in a sharded MongoDB cluster. Users create short links and the service redirects visitors quickly. We also want basic click counts per link.

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: State functional requirements, read/write ratio and storage estimates.
keyPoints: Create short link, optional custom alias and expiry; redirect via 301/302
Approximate click analytics, not real-time exact
Back-of-envelope: ~40 writes/s avg, ~4k redirects/s avg, peaks 10x
Storage: ~6B docs x ~500B = ~3TB before indexes
High availability for redirects matters more than for creation

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define create, redirect and stats endpoints.
keyPoints: POST /links {longUrl, alias?, expiresAt?} -> {code}, with Idempotency-Key header
GET /{code} -> 302 (trackable) or 301 (cacheable) Location
GET /links/{code}/stats -> click counts by day
DELETE /links/{code} for owner, with auth

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Describe the links document, shard key and index choices.
keyPoints: links: {_id: code, longUrl, ownerId, createdAt, expiresAt}
Shard on {_id: 'hashed'} for even distribution; redirect is a targeted single-shard lookup
Unique alias enforced by _id uniqueness, which is guaranteed per shard key
TTL index on expiresAt to purge expired links
Click counts in separate daily bucket docs {code, day, count} via $inc, not on the hot link doc

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show create and redirect paths including code generation and caching.
keyPoints: Code generation: random 7-char base62 (3.5T space) with insert-and-retry on duplicate key
Or counter ranges allocated per app server, encoded base62 (avoids collisions, but predictable)
Redirect path: CDN/edge cache -> Redis cache -> mongos targeted read
Click events sent async to a queue and aggregated in batches
Stateless app servers behind load balancer talking to mongos routers

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Explain shard key reasoning and how reads scale.
keyPoints: Hashed _id avoids the monotonic-key hot shard that a ranged ObjectId or counter would create
Pre-split chunks when creating the collection to avoid initial balancing
Cache hit ratio high due to Zipfian popularity; caches absorb most redirects
Secondary reads with readPreference nearest acceptable for redirects
Ownership queries (list my links) are scatter-gather; add ownerId index or a separate collection sharded by ownerId

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Discuss durability and availability during node or shard failure.
keyPoints: Writes with w:majority so a created link survives primary failover
Retryable writes plus idempotency key prevent duplicate links on client retries
Primary election takes seconds; redirects still served from cache and secondaries
Lost click events tolerable; queue provides buffering
Guard against abuse: malware URL scanning, rate limit creation

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare code generation strategies and redirect status codes.
keyPoints: Random codes: unguessable, needs collision retry; counters: no collision but enumerable
Hashing the long URL gives dedupe but collisions and per-user semantics issues
301 reduces load but loses analytics; 302 keeps tracking
Hashed shard key: even writes but no range queries on code
Key-value store alternative; MongoDB gives secondary indexes and flexible schema

modelSummary: Links are stored as documents keyed by the short code in _id, in a collection sharded on a hashed _id so writes spread evenly and every redirect is a targeted single-shard read. Codes are random 7-character base62 strings inserted with retry on duplicate-key errors, which also makes custom aliases trivially unique. Writes use w:majority and retryable writes, and the API accepts an idempotency key. The redirect path goes through a CDN and Redis cache before hitting mongos, and secondaries can serve cache misses. Click analytics are emitted asynchronously and aggregated into per-day bucket documents with $inc, keeping hot link documents read-only. A TTL index removes expired links. Owner listings use a secondary index or a separate owner-sharded collection to avoid scatter-gather. The main trade-offs are 301 vs 302 and random vs counter codes.

title: Design a feature-flag service
brief: Design a feature-flag service used by hundreds of internal microservices and our client apps. Engineers define flags with targeting rules and percentage rollouts, and changes should propagate within seconds. Flag evaluation must never take down the calling service.
constraints: ~5k flags, rules evaluated millions of times per second in aggregate
Audit history of all changes required

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define flag types, targeting, propagation and audit needs.
keyPoints: Boolean and multivariate flags with rules on user attributes and segments
Percentage rollouts sticky per user via deterministic hashing
Change propagation under 5s; evaluation local to the SDK
Audit log, approvals for production changes, kill switch
Out of scope: experiment statistics engine

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Specify the management API and the SDK interface.
keyPoints: Admin: PUT /flags/{key} with version field for optimistic concurrency
SDK: isEnabled(flagKey, context, default) evaluated locally
Streaming endpoint GET /stream (SSE) pushing ruleset deltas with version numbers
GET /snapshot?env=prod returning full ruleset and version for bootstrap

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model flags, rules, environments and audit records.
keyPoints: flags: {key, env, version, variations, rules[], rolloutSalt, updatedBy}
Rule = ordered clauses on attributes plus percentage weights
Audit collection append-only {flagKey, beforeVersion, after, actor, ts}
Update flag and insert audit record in one multi-document transaction, or use an outbox

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show how changes flow from admin to every SDK.
keyPoints: Admin service writes flags to MongoDB replica set with w:majority
Change stream on the flags collection feeds a publisher that pushes deltas
Edge relay/streaming tier fans out over SSE; CDN-hosted snapshot for bootstrap
SDK holds ruleset in memory and evaluates with hash(flagKey + salt + userId) mod 100
Resume tokens let the publisher continue after restart without missing changes

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Explain how the read fan-out scales to many SDKs.
keyPoints: Ruleset is small (MBs); replicate fully, no sharding needed
Relay nodes scale horizontally; each holds many SSE connections
Snapshots cached on CDN keyed by env+version
Delta-only pushes; SDK requests full snapshot on version gap

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Describe behaviour when the service or network is unavailable.
keyPoints: SDK keeps serving last known ruleset; persists it to local disk for cold starts
Hardcoded default returned if no ruleset ever loaded
Change stream resume token invalid (oplog rolled over) -> republish full snapshot
Bad flag change mitigated by versioned rollback and staged rollout of config
Reconnect with jittered exponential backoff to avoid thundering herd

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare local vs remote evaluation and push vs poll.
keyPoints: Local evaluation: fast and resilient, but ruleset visible to clients (hide for mobile/web)
Remote evaluation for untrusted clients: secure but adds latency
Push (SSE) gives seconds latency; polling simpler but slower and wasteful
Eventual consistency across SDKs: brief windows where instances disagree

modelSummary: Flags and their rules are stored in a MongoDB replica set, each flag carrying a version used for optimistic concurrency, with every change recorded in an append-only audit collection within the same transaction. A publisher tails a change stream on the flags collection and pushes versioned deltas through a horizontally scaled relay tier over SSE, while full snapshots are served via a CDN for bootstrap. SDKs evaluate flags in-process against an in-memory ruleset using deterministic hashing for sticky percentage rollouts, so evaluation takes microseconds and never needs a network call. If the service is unreachable, SDKs keep the last known ruleset, persisted to disk, and fall back to coded defaults. Version gaps or invalid resume tokens trigger a full snapshot resync. Untrusted clients use server-side evaluation so rules are not exposed. The design accepts a few seconds of eventual consistency in exchange for resilience and speed.

title: Design a global leaderboard
brief: Design a leaderboard for a mobile game with tens of millions of players. Players submit scores after each match and want to see their global rank, the top 100, and players near them. There are also weekly leaderboards that reset.
constraints: Rank freshness within a few seconds

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define ranking semantics, tie-breaking and freshness.
keyPoints: Best score per player per board; ties broken by earliest achievement time
Queries: top N, my rank, neighbours around me
All-time and weekly boards; possibly per-region boards
Exact rank for top ranks; approximate rank acceptable deep in the tail
Anti-cheat validation of scores out of scope but hooks needed

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define submit and query endpoints.
keyPoints: POST /boards/{id}/scores {playerId, score, matchId} idempotent by matchId
GET /boards/{id}/top?n=100
GET /boards/{id}/players/{pid}/rank -> {rank, score}
GET /boards/{id}/players/{pid}/around?k=5

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Describe the ranking structure and system of record.
keyPoints: Redis sorted set per board: ZADD GT keeps max; ZREVRANK gives rank in O(log N)
Encode tie-break into score: score * 2^k + (MAX_TS - ts)
System of record in MongoDB: {boardId, playerId, bestScore, achievedAt} unique index on (boardId, playerId)
Weekly boards keyed by week id; old keys expire

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show write and read paths and how the cache is rebuilt.
keyPoints: Submit path: validate, upsert best score in MongoDB with $max, then ZADD to Redis
Or emit to a log and have consumers update Redis, giving replayability
Top 100 cached and refreshed every second
Redis rebuildable from MongoDB if lost

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Handle a single 50M-member sorted set and high write rate.
keyPoints: A 50M sorted set (~5GB) fits one Redis node but is a hot key; replicate for reads
Alternative: shard by score range; rank = count in higher shards + local rank
Or shard by player hash and compute approximate rank via score histogram buckets
Batch writes to Redis; only write when score improves
MongoDB sharded on hashed playerId for the record store

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Consider data loss, replay and reset correctness.
keyPoints: Redis failover may drop recent updates; replay from log or MongoDB
Idempotent submissions via matchId prevent double counting
Weekly reset by switching to a new key rather than deleting in place
Degrade to cached stale ranks if ranking tier is unavailable

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare exact vs approximate rank and storage options.
keyPoints: Exact global rank needs a single ordered structure or cross-shard counting
Histogram approximation scales easily but rank is +/- bucket width
Database index on score with countDocuments is too slow at this rate
Write-through vs log-driven updates: simplicity vs replayability

modelSummary: Each board is a Redis sorted set where ZADD with GT keeps a player's best score and ZREVRANK and ZREVRANGE answer my-rank, top-N and neighbour queries in logarithmic time. Ties are broken by packing achievement time into the score. MongoDB, sharded by hashed playerId, is the durable system of record, updated with $max upserts, and Redis can be rebuilt from it or from a score event log. Submissions are idempotent by matchId. The 50M-entry set fits in memory, so read replicas absorb query load, and the top 100 is cached. If write load or size outgrows one node, the board is split by score range, with rank computed as the counts of higher ranges plus local rank, or approximated with histograms for tail players. Weekly boards use a new key per week, which makes the reset atomic and lets old boards expire.

title: Design a notification fan-out service
brief: Design a service that sends notifications through push, email and SMS on behalf of other product teams. Some notifications go to one user, while others such as announcements go to millions. Users have preferences and quiet hours, and we must not spam them or send duplicates.
constraints: Average 5k notifications/s, bursts of 10M recipients for a broadcast
Third-party providers (APNs, FCM, email/SMS vendors) have rate limits
At-least-once internally with no visible duplicates

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define channels, priorities, preferences and delivery guarantees.
keyPoints: Channels push/email/SMS/in-app; templates with localisation
Priority classes: transactional (OTP, security) vs marketing/broadcast
User preferences, opt-outs, quiet hours, frequency caps
Deduplication and delivery status tracking
Provider throttling and retries

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define send, broadcast and status APIs.
keyPoints: POST /notifications {userId, template, params, channels, priority, idempotencyKey}
POST /broadcasts {segmentId, template, schedule}
GET /notifications/{id} -> status per channel
Webhooks from providers for delivery receipts

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model notifications, preferences and device tokens.
keyPoints: notifications: {_id, userId, idemKey, channel, status, attempts} unique index on idemKey
preferences and device tokens per user, sharded by userId
Broadcast job doc with cursor/progress per partition
TTL index to expire delivered notification records after N days

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show the pipeline from request to provider.
keyPoints: API writes request and enqueues to Kafka topics split by priority
Fan-out workers expand segments into per-user messages in pages
Preference/filter stage then per-channel sender workers
Per-provider token-bucket rate limiting and connection pooling
Status updates written back from provider callbacks

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Explain how broadcasts and hot paths scale.
keyPoints: Partition queues by userId for ordering per user
Broadcasts split into segment chunks processed in parallel
Separate queues so broadcasts never starve transactional traffic
Backpressure: senders slow consumption when providers throttle (429s)

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Discuss retries, duplicates and provider outages.
keyPoints: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter; DLQ after max attempts
Dedupe check via idempotency key before sending to provider
Failover to secondary SMS/email vendor
Remove invalid device tokens on provider feedback
Broadcast progress checkpointed to resume after crash

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare fan-out strategies and guarantees.
keyPoints: Exactly-once to external providers impossible; at-least-once plus dedupe
Fan-out on write vs pull-based in-app inbox for broadcasts
Single queue simpler but priority inversion risk
Batching provider calls improves throughput but adds latency

modelSummary: Producers call an API that records each request with an idempotency key and enqueues it on Kafka topics separated by priority, so broadcasts cannot starve transactional messages. Broadcast jobs are expanded in checkpointed pages by fan-out workers into per-user messages, which pass through a preference stage applying opt-outs, quiet hours and frequency caps. Per-channel senders call APNs, FCM and email/SMS vendors behind per-provider token buckets, and they apply backpressure when providers throttle. Delivery is at-least-once internally, and a unique-indexed notification record prevents visible duplicates. Failures retry with jittered backoff and then go to a DLQ, and secondary vendors provide failover. Provider receipts update status, invalid tokens are pruned, and a TTL index ages out old records. In-app broadcasts can use a pull model to avoid writing millions of rows.

title: Design a chat/messaging system using MongoDB change streams
brief: Design a chat backend supporting 1:1 and group conversations, with messages stored in MongoDB. Online users should receive new messages in real time, and offline users should catch up when they reconnect. Discuss how you would use change streams and where they stop being the right tool.
constraints: Per-conversation ordering required; history retained indefinitely

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Specify messaging semantics, ordering, receipts and history.
keyPoints: Send/receive in 1:1 and groups; per-conversation total order
Offline sync via cursor; read receipts and typing indicators (ephemeral)
At-least-once delivery with client-side dedupe by message id
Message history pagination
Out of scope: E2E encryption details, media transcoding

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define WebSocket events and REST endpoints.
keyPoints: WS send {convId, clientMsgId, body} -> ack {msgId, seq}
WS push message events to recipients
GET /conversations/{id}/messages?afterSeq=&limit= for sync
POST /conversations/{id}/read {seq}

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model conversations, messages and per-user state.
keyPoints: messages: {convId, seq, senderId, body, ts} with unique index {convId, seq}
Shard messages on {convId: 1, seq: 1} or hashed convId so a conversation's history is co-located
seq allocated by $inc on conversation doc with findOneAndUpdate
Membership: per-user inbox {userId, convId, lastReadSeq} sharded by userId
clientMsgId unique per sender for idempotent retries

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show how a message flows from sender to online recipients.
keyPoints: Gateway tier holds WebSockets; presence registry maps userId -> gateway node
Send: write message w:majority, then publish to recipients' gateways via pub/sub or Kafka
Change streams (require replica set; via mongos on sharded clusters) useful for derived consumers
Avoid every gateway opening a filtered change stream; does not scale to thousands of watchers
Offline users pull by lastSeq on reconnect; mobile push for offline

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Discuss partitioning and fan-out for large groups.
keyPoints: Messages write once per conversation, fan-out on read for groups
Presence-based routing sends only to gateways with online members
A small number of change stream consumers partitioned by convId hash, then routed
Hot conversation risk limited because seq doc contention caps per-conv throughput; acceptable

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Explain behaviour on gateway crashes, failovers and duplicates.
keyPoints: Change stream resume tokens persisted so consumers restart without gaps
majority write concern ensures acked messages survive failover; change streams only emit majority-committed changes
Client dedupes by msgId and fills gaps with seq-based sync
Gateway crash: clients reconnect elsewhere and resync from lastSeq

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare change streams vs explicit message bus, and seq strategies.
keyPoints: Change streams: no dual-write, but limited fan-out and oplog-window dependency
Kafka/outbox: scalable routing, more infrastructure
Per-conversation seq counter vs ObjectId/timestamp ordering
Fan-out on write (inbox per user) vs on read for large groups

modelSummary: Messages are stored once per conversation in a collection sharded by conversation id, with a per-conversation sequence number allocated atomically through findOneAndUpdate with $inc and a unique {convId, seq} index for ordering and idempotency. Writes use w:majority before the sender is acked. Clients hold WebSockets to a gateway tier, and a presence registry maps users to gateways. A small, partitioned set of change stream consumers (change streams need a replica set or sharded cluster and only emit majority-committed changes) reads new messages and routes them to the gateways of online members, persisting resume tokens so restarts lose nothing. Offline users receive mobile push and resync by last seen seq when they reconnect. Clients dedupe by message id and fill gaps using seq. At higher fan-out, a transactional outbox into Kafka replaces direct change stream routing, because thousands of watchers per cluster do not scale.

title: Design a distributed job scheduler
brief: Design a service that lets teams schedule jobs to run once at a given time or on a cron schedule, and then executes them on a worker fleet. Jobs must not be lost and should not run twice concurrently. Think about what happens when workers or schedulers crash mid-job.
constraints: 100M scheduled jobs, 10k job triggers/s peak (top of the minute spikes)
Trigger within 1s of the scheduled time
At-least-once execution with idempotent handlers expected

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define scheduling semantics and execution guarantees.
keyPoints: One-off and cron jobs; timezone-aware schedules
At-least-once execution, no concurrent duplicate runs of the same job
Retries with backoff, timeouts, cancellation
Per-tenant quotas and priorities
Execution history visible to users

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define job management and worker APIs.
keyPoints: POST /jobs {schedule, payload, handler, retryPolicy, idempotencyKey}
DELETE /jobs/{id}, GET /jobs/{id}/runs
Worker: lease(batch) -> runs; heartbeat(runId); complete(runId, result)
Fencing token returned with each lease

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model jobs, runs and leases.
keyPoints: jobs: {_id, tenantId, nextRunAt, cron, state, version}
Index {state, nextRunAt} for due-job scanning; shard by bucket of hashed jobId
runs: {jobId, scheduledFor, status, leaseOwner, leaseExpiresAt, attempt, fencingToken}
Unique index {jobId, scheduledFor} so a trigger produces exactly one run record

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show schedulers, queue and workers.
keyPoints: Scheduler partitions each own a set of job buckets and poll due jobs
Claim atomically with findOneAndUpdate setting state and advancing nextRunAt
Push runs to a queue; workers lease with visibility timeout and heartbeat
Partition ownership via leader election/leases (e.g. etcd or lease docs)
Time-wheel or in-memory near-term buffer to hit 1s precision

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Explain how triggering and execution scale, including minute spikes.
keyPoints: Partition job space into N buckets; rebalance buckets across schedulers
Prefetch jobs due in the next minute to smooth top-of-minute spikes
Encourage jitter on cron schedules
Per-tenant concurrency enforced at lease time to avoid noisy neighbours

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Cover crashes, lease expiry, duplicates and clock issues.
keyPoints: Worker crash: lease expires, run reassigned with new attempt
Zombie worker: fencing token checked by downstream on writes
Scheduler crash: partition lease taken over; idempotent run creation via unique index
Missed-schedule policy on recovery: fire once vs catch up all
Rely on DB time or bounded clock skew for leases

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare polling DB vs delay queues, and guarantees.
keyPoints: DB polling: simple, durable, index-scan load; delay queue: precise but harder to cancel/edit
Exactly-once execution infeasible; at-least-once plus idempotent handlers and fencing
Centralized scheduler simpler but SPOF; partitioned adds rebalancing complexity
Lease length: short = fast recovery but more heartbeats

modelSummary: Jobs are stored with a nextRunAt field and indexed by state and due time, and the job space is split into buckets that scheduler instances own through leases. Each scheduler prefetches jobs coming due, then atomically claims them with findOneAndUpdate, which advances nextRunAt for cron jobs and inserts a run record whose unique {jobId, scheduledFor} index makes trigger creation idempotent even if two schedulers race. Runs go to a queue, and workers lease them with a visibility timeout, heartbeat, and a monotonically increasing fencing token that downstream systems check so that zombie workers cannot commit. Expired leases are retried with backoff up to a limit and then dead-lettered. Per-tenant concurrency is enforced at lease time. Execution is at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent, and a missed-run policy controls catch-up after outages. Prefetching and schedule jitter smooth spikes at the top of each minute.

title: Design a metrics/time-series ingestion system with MongoDB time series collections
brief: Design a metrics platform that ingests measurements from hundreds of thousands of hosts and supports dashboards and alerting. Store the data in MongoDB time series collections. Explain retention, downsampling, and how you keep queries fast as data grows.

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define ingestion, query patterns, retention and alerting needs.
keyPoints: Ingest numeric samples with tags (host, service, region)
Queries: range scan by metric+tags, aggregations over time windows
Tiered retention with downsampling
Handle late and out-of-order points
High-cardinality tags (e.g. request id) should be rejected or limited

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define ingestion and query interfaces.
keyPoints: POST /ingest batched points, compressed, from agents
Query API: metric, tag filters, time range, step, aggregation
Alert rule CRUD and evaluation status
Agents retry with backoff and buffer locally

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Describe the time series collection configuration.
keyPoints: Time series collection with timeField ts, metaField meta {metric, host, service}
granularity 'seconds' (or bucketMaxSpanSeconds tuned) matching ingest rate
Internally buckets points by meta and time for compression and columnar storage
expireAfterSeconds for raw retention; separate rollup collection for 1-minute aggregates
Secondary compound index on meta fields and ts for dashboard queries

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show path from agent to storage and query.
keyPoints: Agents -> ingest gateways -> Kafka partitioned by series -> writer consumers
Writers batch insertMany unordered, w:1 or w:majority depending on durability needs
Rollup jobs using $setWindowFields/$group with $merge into rollup collection
Query service routes to raw or rollup collection by range
Alert evaluator reads recent data or consumes the stream directly

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Explain sharding and write throughput.
keyPoints: Shard time series collection on metaField subfields (e.g. meta.host) not on time alone
Time-only shard key creates a hot shard on the latest chunk
Grouping writes by series improves bucket fill and compression
Cardinality limits protect bucket count and index size
Kafka absorbs bursts; consumers scale with partitions

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Discuss backpressure, data loss and late data.
keyPoints: Kafka retention allows replay after writer or DB outage
Backpressure to agents with 429 and local buffering
Late points inserted into older buckets; rollups recomputed for affected windows
Primary failover: retryable writes; idempotent duplicates tolerable or deduped by key

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare with purpose-built TSDBs and different durability levels.
keyPoints: Time series collections give compression and query language; specialised TSDBs may compress better
w:1 boosts throughput but risks losing acked points on failover
Pre-aggregation reduces query cost but loses detail
Updates/deletes on time series collections are more limited than regular collections

modelSummary: Agents batch and compress samples to stateless ingest gateways, which publish them into Kafka partitioned by series so bursts are absorbed and data can be replayed. Writer consumers issue unordered insertMany calls into a MongoDB time series collection with ts as the timeField and the metric and tags as the metaField. MongoDB buckets points per series and time range in columnar, compressed form. Granularity is set to match the ingest rate. The collection is sharded on metaField subfields such as host, because a time-based shard key would send all writes to the newest chunk. Raw data expires after 15 days through expireAfterSeconds, and periodic aggregation pipelines use $merge to write one-minute rollups to a separate collection kept for 13 months, recomputing windows that receive late data. The query service picks raw or rollup data based on the requested range, and alerting evaluates recent windows. Tag cardinality limits protect the index and bucket counts.

title: Design a change-data-capture pipeline from MongoDB to a search index
brief: Our product catalog lives in a sharded MongoDB cluster, and we need it searchable in Elasticsearch or Atlas Search-like infrastructure with near real-time freshness. Design the CDC pipeline, including the initial backfill and how to keep the index correct through failures and schema changes.
constraints: Zero lost updates; index must converge to source of truth
Backfill must not hurt production latency
Documents up to 100KB with nested arrays

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define correctness, freshness and transformation needs.
keyPoints: Every insert/update/delete reflected in index eventually, in order per document
Initial snapshot plus continuous streaming
Transform/denormalise documents into search schema
Reindex on mapping changes without downtime
Observability: lag and reconciliation metrics

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Describe internal interfaces between pipeline stages.
keyPoints: Change event envelope {_id, op, fullDocument, clusterTime, resumeToken}
Admin API: start backfill, pause, reindex to new alias
Search API reads via alias so index swaps are atomic

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Describe event content and checkpoint storage.
keyPoints: Change stream with fullDocument: 'updateLookup' (or post-images) to get full state
Checkpoint store: last processed resume token per stream
Index doc id = MongoDB _id; external versioning with clusterTime to reject stale writes
Deletes as tombstones mapped to index deletes

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show capture, transport, transform and sink.
keyPoints: Single change stream via mongos (merges shards in cluster time order) or per-shard streams
Publish to Kafka keyed by _id to preserve per-document order
Transform workers build search docs; bulk index with retries
Backfill: record start operationTime, scan collection from secondaries, then stream with startAtOperationTime
Alias-based blue/green reindex for mapping changes

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Explain throughput scaling and backfill isolation.
keyPoints: Kafka partitions by _id hash allow parallel consumers with per-key ordering
Bulk requests sized by bytes; tune refresh interval
Backfill reads from secondary or hidden/analytics nodes with readPreference secondary
Rate-limit backfill to protect primary and oplog

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Cover resume, oplog rollover and idempotency.
keyPoints: Persist resume token only after Kafka ack: at-least-once capture
Idempotent sink via doc id and version (clusterTime) so replays and reorderings are safe
If resume token falls off the oplog window, trigger re-snapshot; size oplog accordingly
updateLookup returns current doc, not doc at event time; versioning handles it
Periodic reconciliation comparing counts/hashes

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare capture approaches and consistency.
keyPoints: Change streams vs application dual-writes (inconsistent) vs transactional outbox
updateLookup costs an extra read; pre/post images use storage
Kafka adds durability and fan-out but more moving parts
Atlas Search keeps index in sync natively, reducing custom code

modelSummary: A capture service opens a change stream on the catalog collection through mongos, which merges shard events in cluster-time order. It uses fullDocument updateLookup or post-images so each event carries the full document state, and publishes events to Kafka keyed by _id to keep per-document ordering. The resume token is checkpointed only after Kafka acknowledges the write, which gives at-least-once capture. Transform workers denormalise documents and bulk-index them, using _id as the index id and the event clusterTime as an external version so that replayed or out-of-order events cannot overwrite newer data. Deletes become index deletes. The initial backfill records an operationTime, scans a secondary at a limited rate, and then streams from that point, so the snapshot and the stream overlap safely. Oplog sizing covers the longest expected outage, and losing the resume token triggers a re-snapshot. Mapping changes build a new index behind an alias and swap atomically, and periodic reconciliation verifies convergence.

title: Design a multi-region user profile store
brief: Design a user profile service for a global product with users in North America, Europe and Asia. Reads must be fast everywhere, some users' data must stay in their region for compliance, and the service should survive a full region outage. Discuss consistency carefully.
constraints: EU users' data must reside in the EU (GDPR)
RPO 0 for acknowledged writes, RTO < 1 minute for a region loss
Users mostly access from their home region but travel

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define consistency, residency and availability goals.
keyPoints: Read-your-writes for the user themselves; others may read slightly stale
Data residency by home region
Survive region failure without losing acked writes
Profile reads dominate; writes small partial updates
Account deletion propagated everywhere

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define profile endpoints and consistency hints.
keyPoints: GET /users/{id}/profile, PATCH /users/{id}/profile with If-Match version
Session token carries homeRegion and last write operationTime
Router sends request to home region when needed

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Describe the document and shard key with location.
keyPoints: profiles: {_id: userId, region, version, ...attributes}
Shard key {region: 1, _id: 1} with zone sharding pinning region ranges to region shards
Each zone's replica set has members across 3 AZs (or nearby regions) for majority survival
Version field for optimistic concurrency

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show global routing and replica placement.
keyPoints: Global sharded cluster; zones map EU/NA/APAC ranges to shards with primaries in-region
Writes w:majority to home-region primary
Local reads readPreference nearest; read-your-writes via causally consistent sessions or reading home primary after writes
Non-resident data may have read-only secondaries in other regions only where allowed
GeoDNS sends users to nearest app tier

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Discuss scaling per region and traveling users.
keyPoints: Each zone scales independently by adding shards within the zone
Hashed component in shard key inside region avoids hot chunks
Travelling users: cross-region read to home or cached copy; writes go to home
Edge cache of non-sensitive public fields with short TTL

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Explain region failure and the RPO/RTO trade.
keyPoints: RPO 0 requires majority across failure domains; 2-1-2 across three regions survives one region loss
Writes then pay cross-region latency; within-region-AZ majority is faster but region loss loses availability
Automatic election gives RTO of seconds
Residency limits where voting members can live (EU in multiple EU regions)
Retryable writes absorb failover errors

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare single-writer per user vs multi-writer.
keyPoints: Home-region single writer avoids conflicts; multi-master needs CRDT/LWW conflict resolution
Stronger consistency means higher write latency (PACELC)
Causal consistency is cheaper than linearizable reads everywhere
Per-region separate clusters simplify compliance but complicate global queries

modelSummary: Profiles are stored in one globally sharded MongoDB cluster with the shard key {region, _id}, and zone sharding pins each region's key range to shards whose primaries sit in that region, which satisfies residency and keeps writes local. Each zone's replica set spreads voting members across failure domains within the allowed geography, for example three EU regions, so majority-acknowledged writes survive a region loss with RPO 0 and automatic elections give an RTO of seconds. The cost is cross-region write latency. Writes always go to the home primary with w:majority and optimistic concurrency on a version field. Reads use nearest secondaries for speed, and the user's own read-your-writes is guaranteed through causally consistent sessions or by routing reads to the primary right after a write. Travelling users read and write through their home region. A single writer per user avoids the conflict resolution that a multi-master design would need. Non-sensitive fields can be cached at the edge.

title: Design collaborative document sync
brief: Design the backend for a collaborative editor like Google Docs, where many people edit the same document simultaneously and also edit offline. Edits must converge to the same result for everyone without losing work. Explain your choice of conflict-resolution approach and how you persist documents.
constraints: Up to 100 simultaneous editors per document
Offline edits of hours must merge cleanly

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define convergence, latency, offline and history needs.
keyPoints: Real-time co-editing with presence and cursors
Strong eventual consistency: all replicas converge to same state
Offline editing and merge on reconnect
Version history and restore
Permissions per document

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define sync protocol messages.
keyPoints: WS: join(docId, stateVector) -> missing ops/snapshot
WS: ops {docId, clientId, clock, ops[]} broadcast to peers, ack with server seq
GET /docs/{id}/versions, POST /docs/{id}/restore

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Describe how operations and snapshots are stored.
keyPoints: Append-only ops log {docId, seq, clientId, clock, payload} unique {docId, seq}
Periodic snapshots {docId, seq, state} to bound replay
Shard on docId (hashed) so a doc's log is co-located
Compaction of old ops into snapshots while keeping history checkpoints

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show session routing and persistence.
keyPoints: Route all editors of a doc to one session server via consistent hashing on docId
Session server holds doc state in memory, sequences ops, broadcasts
OT requires central server transform; CRDT (e.g. RGA/Yjs) merges commutatively
Persist ops before ack (w:majority) then broadcast
Presence/cursors ephemeral and not persisted

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Discuss session server scaling and hot documents.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing with rebalancing on node changes
Batch ops per few ms to reduce writes and broadcast frames
Very hot docs: read-only viewers served by fan-out relays
Snapshot loading from object storage for large docs

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Cover server crash, reconnection and duplicates.
keyPoints: Session server crash: new owner loads snapshot + ops tail; clients resend unacked ops
Idempotency via (clientId, clock) dedupe
Ownership lease with fencing so two servers do not both sequence a doc
Client keeps local op queue for offline and replays on reconnect

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare OT and CRDT approaches.
keyPoints: OT: compact ops, needs central sequencer, tricky correctness
CRDT: offline/P2P friendly, metadata overhead and tombstones
Single owner per doc simplifies ordering but is a scaling unit limit
Snapshot frequency trades storage vs load time

modelSummary: All editors of a document connect to one session server selected by consistent hashing on the document id, and that server holds the document in memory under an ownership lease with fencing. Clients send operations tagged with clientId and a logical clock, and the server dedupes them, assigns a sequence number, appends them to an operation log in MongoDB sharded by docId with w:majority, and then acks and broadcasts. A CRDT such as a Yjs/RGA-style sequence is used so that concurrent and long offline edits merge commutatively and converge without a central transform, at the cost of metadata and tombstones. Periodic snapshots bound replay time and act as version-history checkpoints, while older operations are compacted. When a server crashes, a new owner loads the latest snapshot and the log tail, and clients resend unacknowledged operations, which are deduped. Presence and cursors are ephemeral. OT is a valid alternative if the system stays server-centric and offline support is limited.

title: Design an online backup and restore service for a database
brief: Design a managed backup service for customers' MongoDB replica sets and sharded clusters, similar to what a cloud database provider offers. It should take consistent backups without downtime and support point-in-time restore to any second within the retention window. Sharded clusters must restore to a consistent cluster-wide point.
constraints: Point-in-time restore granularity of 1 second within 7 days
Snapshots daily, retained 30 days; RPO for PITR ~ seconds
Backup must add < 5% overhead on production nodes

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define consistency, retention and restore semantics.
keyPoints: Consistent snapshots for replica sets and causally consistent cluster-wide snapshots for sharded clusters
Continuous oplog capture for PITR
Restore to new cluster or in place; download option
Encryption at rest with customer keys, cross-region copies
Retention policies and immutable backups

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define backup policy and restore operations.
keyPoints: PUT /clusters/{id}/backupPolicy {snapshotSchedule, retention, pitrWindow}
POST /clusters/{id}/restores {targetCluster, pointInTime | snapshotId}
GET /restores/{id} with progress
Async job model with idempotency keys

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Describe snapshot, oplog and metadata storage.
keyPoints: Snapshot files in object storage, content-addressed blocks for incremental dedupe
Oplog slices stored as ordered chunks keyed by (cluster, shard, ts range)
Metadata catalog: snapshots with per-shard timestamps, oplog coverage ranges
Checksums per block for integrity

sections.title: High-level design
sections.prompt: Show snapshot capture, oplog tailing and restore flows.
keyPoints: Snapshots taken from a secondary using WiredTiger backup cursor (or storage snapshot) to avoid primary impact
Oplog tailers per shard continuously ship oplog to object storage
Sharded cluster: pick a cluster time T; each shard restores snapshot then replays oplog to T
Balancer/chunk migrations considered: pause or capture config server state at T
Restore: download blocks in parallel, build data files, replay oplog, then start nodes

sections.title: Scaling & partitioning
sections.prompt: Explain scaling across many clusters and large sizes.
keyPoints: Fleet of stateless backup agents scheduled per cluster/shard
Incremental block-level snapshots so daily cost is proportional to changes
Parallel per-shard restores; 1TB/hour needs ~300MB/s throughput across streams
Throttle snapshot I/O to stay under overhead budget

sections.title: Failure modes & reliability
sections.prompt: Cover oplog gaps, corruption and agent failures.
keyPoints: Detect oplog gaps (tailer falls behind oplog window) and force a new snapshot
Rollbacks: only ship majority-committed oplog entries
Agent crash: resume from last shipped ts, idempotent chunk uploads
Regular automated test restores to validate backups
Immutable object lock to defend against ransomware/deletion

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare logical vs physical backups and snapshot strategies.
keyPoints: mongodump logical backups are portable but slow and inconsistent on sharded clusters without care
Physical/filesystem snapshots are fast but storage-engine coupled
Continuous oplog vs frequent snapshots: storage vs restore time
Restore speed vs storage cost of more frequent full snapshots

modelSummary: A fleet of stateless backup agents takes physical, incremental snapshots of each shard from a secondary using a WiredTiger backup cursor or storage-level snapshots. Data files are split into checksummed, content-addressed blocks in encrypted, immutable object storage, so daily snapshots cost only the changed blocks. Separate tailers ship each shard's majority-committed oplog in ordered chunks to provide one-second point-in-time recovery, and a metadata catalog tracks snapshot timestamps and oplog coverage so gaps are detected and trigger a new snapshot. For sharded clusters, a restore selects one cluster time, restores each shard and the config server from snapshots taken before it, and replays each oplog up to that time, which yields a causally consistent cluster state while chunk migrations are handled through config state. Restores pull blocks in parallel per shard to meet throughput targets. Snapshot I/O is throttled to keep production overhead low, and automated test restores verify that backups actually work.
